messages.author: 51b3abd8ec37025e
messages.subject: separation of transects
parts: Hi.  We estimate density of kangaroos in a number of small nature reserves (1.4 to 20 sq km). Based on initial surveys, we calculated the need for 44 km of transects to get a CV of 15%. When 44 km of transect is laid out in the smaller reserves the transects are very close together, down to 35 m apart. Of course we walk nearby transects on different days but my question is whether there is a minimum separation between transects below which it becomes better to repeat fewer transects, analysing the repeats as such (non-independent). Our species of kangaroo (Eastern Grey) is sedentary and it is possible to see large groups in the same spot at the same time day after day so transects a few metres apart would record much the same on different days.  I could not find any guidance in the Distance books on this and wondered if Effective Strip Width (usually around 100 m either side of the transect in our case) was a reasonable minimum for transect separation, below which the same transect should be repeated if necessary to reach the desired number of detections.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] separation of transects
parts:
Don:

The delay in response is because I don't have any strong guidance to offer on this.  I presume your effort calculations are based upon the equations found in Section 7.2.2 of Buckland et al. (2001).    I bring this up because those equations use a conservative value for "q" of 3.0 in Eqn. 7.1; unless you have computed your own value of q using Eqn 7.2.

There is some discussion of this subject (although it might not be directly related to your issue) in Section 7.8.3 where the issue of repeating transects for purpose of temporal inference, is discussed.

Finally, the advice on survey effort is only a guide and should be tempered by common sense, as you are doing.  Reserves as small as 1.4km^2 can undoubtedly be sampled with less effort than your larger reserves.

I have no adverse reaction to your suggestion about using ESW as an approximate minimum separation distance.
